questions.title: How does the “absmean” quantization function determine the scaling factor γ?
questions.question_body: In the BitNet b1.58 paper the weight quantization is defined as \(\widetilde{W}=\mathrm{RoundClip}(W/(\gamma+\epsilon),-1,1)\) with \(\gamma = \frac{1}{nm}\sum_{ij}|W_{ij}|\). I am confused about why the authors use the average absolute value of the weight matrix as the scaling factor instead of, say, the maximum absolute value or RMS. How does this choice affect the distribution of ternary weights and the stability of training?

questions.title: Why are activations quantized to the symmetric range \([-Q_b, Q_b]\) instead of using a zero‑point offset?
questions.question_body: The paper states that activation quantization is performed per token to \([-Q_b, Q_b]\) to “get rid of the zero‑point quantization”. I don’t understand how removing the zero‑point simplifies implementation and whether it introduces any bias in the activation distribution. Could someone explain the trade‑offs between symmetric and asymmetric quantization in this context?

questions.title: What is the theoretical justification for calling a ternary weight model “1.58‑bit”?
questions.question_body: BitNet b1.58 uses weights taking values in \{-1,0,1\}. The authors claim this corresponds to 1.58 bits per weight in the binary system. How is this number derived (e.g., using entropy of a ternary distribution) and does it assume a particular probability of zero weights? Is there an empirical measurement of actual bits per weight after training?

questions.title: How does BitLinear replace nn.Linear while preserving Transformer functionality?
questions.question_body: The architecture replaces every nn.Linear with BitLinear that operates on ternary weights and 8‑bit activations. I am unclear on how back‑propagation is handled through the non‑differentiable rounding in the quantization step, and whether any straight‑through estimator or custom gradient is used. Also, does BitLinear still support bias terms, and if not, how does removing biases affect model expressivity?

questions.title: Can you clarify how the energy savings (71.4×) for matrix multiplication are calculated?
questions.question_body: Figure 5 in the paper reports a 71.4× reduction in arithmetic‑operation energy on 7 nm chips when comparing BitNet b1.58 (INT8 addition) to FP16 (addition + multiplication). What energy model/values are used for INT8 addition vs. FP16 multiplication? Does this figure account for any overhead from additional control logic or memory accesses needed for ternary weight handling?

questions.title: Why does BitNet b1.58 achieve better zero‑shot accuracy than a larger FP16 LLaMA model at comparable parameter count?
questions.question_body: The results show BitNet b1.58 3.9B outperforming FP16 3B on several benchmarks despite having lower precision weights. Is there an explanation beyond “feature filtering” from the zero weight? Could this be due to regularization effects of quantization or differences in training hyperparameters?

questions.title: What are the implications of using 8‑bit activations for KV‑cache memory in long‑sequence inference?
questions.question_body: The discussion mentions that 8‑bit activations allow doubling context length for the same resources, and suggests possible further compression to 4 bits. How exactly does reducing activation precision impact KV‑cache size and what are the potential accuracy trade‑offs when compressing KV caches beyond 8 bits?

questions.title: How would a 1‑bit Mixture‑of‑Experts (MoE) model be built on top of BitNet b1.58?
questions.question_body: The authors briefly propose 1‑bit MoE LLMs but give no architectural details. Would each expert use its own ternary weight matrix and share the same routing network? How does quantization affect the routing logits, and what changes would be needed in load balancing or expert capacity calculations?

questions.title: Is there any loss in expressivity when all linear layers use ternary weights while embeddings remain full precision?
questions.question_body: BitNet b1.58 keeps embedding layers in full precision but quantizes all subsequent linear projections to ternary values. Could this mismatch cause representational bottlenecks, especially for tasks requiring fine‑grained token embeddings? Has any ablation been performed where embeddings are also ternarized?

questions.title: What does “Pareto improvement” mean in the context of BitNet b1.58’s performance vs. FP16 LLaMA?
questions.question_body: The paper claims BitNet b1.58 is a Pareto improvement over state‑of‑the‑art LLMs because it offers lower latency/memory while matching accuracy. How is Pareto optimality formally evaluated here? Does it consider only these three metrics (accuracy, latency, memory) or also other factors like training cost or hardware compatibility?
